title: Offline detectors called this real unboxing video 35% AI
summary: Offline detectors called a real unboxing video 35% AI; after agent review it came out 97% live. rea-video judges every shot as filmed, AI-generated or coded, and writes up how to remake it: https://github.com/JuneYaooo/rea-video
body_markdown:
One of the example cases in rea-video is a 72-second unboxing video, shot for real on an overhead phone rig with one rug and one camera position. After platform transcoding, offline tools called 35% of it AI. After the agent reviewed the uncertain shots, the verdict came out 97% live-action.

I found that gap the most telling example in the project. Platform recompression wipes out the noise evidence offline tools rely on, so a visual check is needed to get the call right. rea-video, from JuneYaooo/rea-video, answers the question shot by shot: was each one filmed, AI-generated or built in code, and how would you remake it?

## A verdict for every shot

The project sorts footage into seven kinds, each with its own output:

- **Live footage** gets setups and camera positions, framing, camera moves, lighting and colour grade.
- **AI video** gets the evidence, a reverse-engineered prompt per shot, and how to batch shots into generations.
- **Avatar** shots get flagged, with the portrait and audio you would need.
- **3D and animation** get a call on whether to generate with a video model or render from 3D code.
- **Code and template** shots, like kinetic type and UI demos, get layout and motion timing ready to rebuild as a Remotion project.
- **Screen recordings** are marked as material you will have to record yourself.
- **Mixed edits** get each shot judged separately, then reassembled on the original timeline.

Every breakdown also covers captions with timings that export to SRT or ASS, stickers and picture-in-picture, cut points and whether they hit the beat, and audio: human or AI voice, AI or library music with its BPM, and where each sound effect lands.

The examples show why per-shot matters. A 19-second clip with 10 shots mixes AI characters talking, code-built UI and 8 seconds of real screen recording. A 70-second product promo comes out 83% code-driven motion graphics and 12% screen recording, so no video model is needed at all. In a 165-second AI music video, the tool flags the song as AI-generated, and when the vision model called some shots "live-action drama", the agent spotted fake Chinese characters on a scroll and ruled them AI.

## Two outputs, one for you and one for your agent

Each run produces a report as HTML or PDF, written for a person to learn from, and a VIDEO.md file. VIDEO.md is an open format that agents read layer by layer, so an agent answering a narrow question reads only the layer it needs and spends fewer tokens.

You can connect a video-capable model such as Gemini or Doubao by giving the agent its endpoint and key. The project says that makes the live, AI and 3D calls more accurate and adds a reverse-engineered prompt for every shot. Without one it still works, and an agent that can see images checks the uncertain shots itself.

One caution from the examples section is worth repeating. The sample videos in the repo are re-compressed, which strips TikTok and Douyin platform tags, so running them yourself gives different results from the published reports, especially without a vision model. To reproduce the reports, use the original platform downloads.

## The remake side

The other half of the pitch is remaking. A companion recipe, capsule-cinema, generates a new version that keeps the original's camera, motion, pacing and transitions and swaps only the elements you pick. If you remake someone else's ad, the rights questions are yours to answer. I find the breakdown more interesting than the remake, as a way to learn how a video was actually made.

## Running a breakdown

You need ffmpeg and Python 3.10+. In Claude Code or Codex, the whole install is one sentence:

```text
Install https://github.com/JuneYaooo/rea-video, then break down this video: /path/to/video.mp4
```

Reports come back in the language you ask in, Chinese or English. I would start with a video you made yourself, where you already know which shots were real, and see how often the per-shot calls match.
